chapter_text:
CHAPTER 14 — शरीरमाद्यं खलु धर्मसाधनम् (SHARIRAMADYAM KHALU DHARMASADHANAM)

Introduction — शरीरम् आद्यं धर्मसाधनम्

The great poet Kalidasa (कालिदासः) wrote a golden half-line in his epic Kumarasambhava (कुमारसम्भवम्): "शरीरमाद्यं खलु धर्मसाधनम्" — "the body is indeed the first (foremost) instrument of dharma." The words split as शरीरम् (body) + आद्यम् (first) + खलु (indeed) + धर्म-साधनम् (the means/instrument of dharma). The idea is simple but profound: whatever duty (धर्म), work (कर्म), study (अध्ययनम्) or service (सेवा) a person wishes to perform, it can be done only through a healthy body. If the body is weak or diseased, even the noblest wish (मनोरथः) cannot be fulfilled. Therefore the very first duty of every human being is to keep the body clean, strong and healthy. In this lesson (NIOS Secondary Sanskrit, Course 209) we read this famous maxim, learn simple Sanskrit prose about caring for the body, study two or three authentic verses on आरोग्य (health), and draw a little grammar (व्याकरणम्) from the words.

Why the body matters (शरीरस्य महत्त्वम्)

A wise saying declares: "आरोग्यं परमं भाग्यम्" — health is the highest fortune. Wealth, learning, friends and honour are all valuable, but none of them can be enjoyed by a person who is constantly ill. The four aims of life — धर्म (duty), अर्थ (wealth), काम (desire) and मोक्ष (liberation) — all rest upon a healthy body, for "शरीरमाद्यं खलु धर्मसाधनम्." Just as a lamp needs oil to give light, the soul (आत्मा) needs a sound body to act in the world. Hence our ancestors gave careful rules for cleanliness (शौचम्), exercise (व्यायामः), food (आहारः), sleep (निद्रा) and self-control (संयमः). To care for the body is not selfishness; it is the first step of dharma, because only a healthy person can serve family, society and nation.

Simple Sanskrit prose on body-care (सरल-संस्कृत-गद्यम्)

शरीरम् अस्माकं प्रथमं धनम् अस्ति। स्वस्थे शरीरे एव स्वस्थं मनः वसति। यः जनः प्रातःकाले उत्तिष्ठति, स्नानं करोति, शुद्धं वस्त्रं धारयति, नियमेन व्यायामं करोति, हितं मितं च भोजनं खादति, समये च निद्रां गच्छति, सः नीरोगः बलवान् च भवति। नीरोगः जनः स्वकीयं कर्तव्यं सम्यक् करोति, विद्यां पठति, परेषाम् उपकारं च करोति। रोगी तु किमपि कर्तुं न शक्नोति। अतः वयं शरीरस्य रक्षां कुर्मः, स्वच्छतां पालयामः, आलस्यं च त्यजामः।

शब्दार्थ (word meanings): शरीरम् = body; प्रथमम् = first; धनम् = wealth; स्वस्थे = in a healthy (locative); मनः = mind; वसति = dwells; प्रातःकाले = in the early morning; उत्तिष्ठति = rises, gets up; स्नानम् = bath; शुद्धम् = clean, pure; वस्त्रम् = garment; धारयति = wears; नियमेन = regularly, by rule; व्यायामम् = exercise; हितम् = beneficial; मितम् = measured, moderate; भोजनम् = food; खादति = eats; निद्राम् = sleep; नीरोगः = free from disease, healthy; बलवान् = strong; कर्तव्यम् = duty; सम्यक् = properly; उपकारम् = help, service; रोगी = a sick person; रक्षाम् = protection; स्वच्छताम् = cleanliness; आलस्यम् = laziness; त्यजामः = we give up.

Translation: The body is our first wealth. Only in a healthy body does a healthy mind dwell. The person who rises in the early morning, bathes, wears clean clothes, exercises regularly, eats beneficial and moderate food, and sleeps on time, becomes free from disease and strong. A healthy person performs his duty properly, studies, and helps others. But a sick person can do nothing. Therefore we protect the body, maintain cleanliness, and give up laziness.

Moral (सारः): "A sound mind lives in a sound body." Cleanliness, exercise, moderate food, timely sleep and the giving-up of laziness are the true means of health — and health is the foundation of every duty.

Verses on health (आरोग्य-विषयकानि सुभाषितानि)

1) शरीरमाद्यं खलु धर्मसाधनम् ।
   (कालिदासस्य कुमारसम्भवात्)
   शब्दार्थ: शरीरम् = the body; आद्यम् = the first, foremost; खलु = indeed, certainly; धर्मसाधनम् = the instrument/means of dharma (धर्म + साधनम्).
   Translation: The body is indeed the foremost instrument for (the practice of) dharma.
   Theme / Moral: Every duty is accomplished through the body; so guarding one's health is itself the first duty.

2) आरोग्यं परमं भाग्यं स्वास्थ्यं सर्वार्थसाधनम् ।
   शब्दार्थ: आरोग्यम् = health, freedom from disease; परमम् = highest, supreme; भाग्यम् = fortune, blessing; स्वास्थ्यम् = well-being, sound health; सर्वार्थसाधनम् = the means to all aims (सर्व + अर्थ + साधनम्).
   Translation: Health is the highest fortune; sound well-being is the means (of achieving) all the aims (of life).
   Theme / Moral: Without health no goal — wealth, learning or happiness — can be reached; therefore health is the greatest treasure.

3) अजीर्णे भेषजं वारि जीर्णे वारि बलप्रदम् ।
   भोजने चामृतं वारि भोजनान्ते विषप्रदम् ॥
   शब्दार्थ: अजीर्णे = in (a state of) indigestion; भेषजम् = medicine; वारि = water; जीर्णे = when (the food is) digested; बलप्रदम् = strength-giving; भोजने = during a meal; अमृतम् = nectar; भोजनान्ते = at the very end of a meal (भोजन + अन्ते); विषप्रदम् = poison-giving.
   Translation: In indigestion water is medicine; when food is digested water gives strength; taken during a meal water is like nectar; taken right at the end of a meal it acts like poison.
   Theme / Moral: Even a common thing like water helps or harms according to the right measure and time — discipline (संयमः) in eating and drinking protects health.

4) व्यायामात् लभते स्वास्थ्यं दीर्घायुष्यं बलं सुखम् ।
   शब्दार्थ: व्यायामात् = from exercise (ablative); लभते = obtains, gets; स्वास्थ्यम् = health; दीर्घायुष्यम् = long life (दीर्घ + आयुष्यम्); बलम् = strength; सुखम् = happiness, ease.
   Translation: From (regular) exercise one obtains health, long life, strength and happiness.
   Theme / Moral: Daily व्यायाम (exercise) is a simple habit that gives health, long life and strength — the body must be kept active, not idle.

A rule for eating (भोजन-नियमः): the tradition praises one who is हितभुक् (eats what is wholesome), मितभुक् (eats in moderation) and ऋतभुक् (eats honestly-earned, pure food). Over-eating (अतिभोजनम्) breeds disease; moderation (मितता) breeds health.

व्याकरणम् — A little grammar from the lesson (English explanation, Devanagari examples)

(A) सन्धि (Sandhi — the joining of sounds). When two sounds meet, they often combine. Examples drawn from this lesson:
  • शरीरम् + आद्यम् → शरीरमाद्यम् (म् joins with the following आ). Split it back as शरीरम् + आद्यम् (सन्धि-विच्छेद).
  • भोजने + अमृतम् → भोजने चामृतम् here च + अमृतम् → चामृतम् (अ + अ = आ, दीर्घ-सन्धि).
  • भोजन + अन्ते → भोजनान्ते (अ + अ = आ, दीर्घ-सन्धि) — "at the end of the meal."
  • दीर्घ + आयुष्यम् → दीर्घायुष्यम् (अ + आ = आ, दीर्घ-सन्धि) — "long life."
  • सर्व + अर्थ → सर्वार्थ (अ + अ = आ) as in सर्वार्थसाधनम्.
Splitting a joined form back into its parts (सन्धि-विच्छेद) is a key reading skill.

(B) विभक्ति (Vibhakti — case endings). Sanskrit nouns change their ending to show their role. Using examples from the lesson:
  • प्रथमा (nominative, the subject): शरीरम् "the body (is)", आरोग्यम् "health (is)". A neuter -अ stem noun has the same form in प्रथमा and द्वितीया singular (शरीरम्).
  • द्वितीया (accusative, the object): व्यायामम् "exercise (as object)", भोजनम् "food", रक्षाम् "protection" — "we do PROTECTION of the body."
  • तृतीया (instrumental, "by/with"): नियमेन "by rule/regularly."
  • पञ्चमी (ablative, "from"): व्यायामात् "FROM exercise."
  • सप्तमी (locative, "in/at"): स्वस्थे शरीरे "in a healthy body", अजीर्णे "in indigestion", भोजने "during a meal."

(C) शब्दरूप (declension — worked example). The neuter word शरीर (ending in अ) declines in प्रथमा through the three numbers as: एकवचन शरीरम् (one body), द्विवचन शरीरे (two bodies), बहुवचन शरीराणि (many bodies). Notice that neuter प्रथमा and द्वितीया forms are alike, so शरीरम् serves as both subject and object. Compare the neuter word फलम् (fruit): फलम् / फले / फलानि — शरीर follows the same pattern.

(D) धातुरूप (conjugation — worked example). The verb-root रक्ष् ("to protect") in लट्-लकार (present tense, परस्मैपद) runs: एकवचन रक्षति (he/she protects), द्विवचन रक्षतः (the two protect), बहुवचन रक्षन्ति (they protect). So "he protects the body" is सः शरीरं रक्षति. Likewise the root खाद् ("to eat") gives खादति / खादतः / खादन्ति, and भू ("to be/become") gives भवति / भवतः / भवन्ति (as in नीरोगः भवति, "he becomes healthy").

SUMMARY (सारांश)

In this chapter you learned Kalidasa's famous maxim "शरीरमाद्यं खलु धर्मसाधनम्" — the body is the first instrument of dharma — and understood that every duty, study and service depends on a healthy body. You read simple Sanskrit prose describing the daily habits of a healthy person: rising early, bathing, wearing clean clothes, regular exercise (व्यायामः), beneficial and moderate food (हितं मितं भोजनम्), timely sleep, and the giving-up of laziness (आलस्यम्). You studied authentic verses on आरोग्य: "आरोग्यं परमं भाग्यम्" (health is the highest fortune), the water-and-digestion verse "अजीर्णे भेषजं वारि..." (the right measure and time make even water a medicine or a poison), and "व्यायामात् लभते स्वास्थ्यम्..." (exercise gives health, long life, strength and happiness), together with the eating-rule हितभुक्-मितभुक्-ऋतभुक्. Finally you drew grammar from the words — सन्धि (शरीरम् + आद्यम् = शरीरमाद्यम्; दीर्घ + आयुष्यम् = दीर्घायुष्यम्) and सन्धि-विच्छेद, the common विभक्ति case-endings, the शब्दरूप of the neuter noun शरीर (शरीरम् / शरीरे / शरीराणि), and the धातुरूप of रक्ष् (रक्षति / रक्षतः / रक्षन्ति). Remember always: guard your body, for it is the foundation of every good deed.

topics.name: शरीरमाद्यं खलु धर्मसाधनम् — The Body as the First Instrument of Dharma
topics.description: Kalidasa's maxim 'शरीरमाद्यं खलु धर्मसाधनम्' (from the Kumarasambhava): its word-split (शरीरम् + आद्यम् + खलु + धर्मसाधनम्), meaning, and the idea that every duty, study and service is accomplished only through a healthy body.

topics.name: आरोग्यम् / स्वास्थ्यम् — Health and its Importance
topics.description: Why health (आरोग्यम्) is called the highest fortune ('आरोग्यं परमं भाग्यम्'); how the four aims धर्म, अर्थ, काम, मोक्ष all rest on a sound body; and health as the foundation of service to family, society and nation.

topics.name: शरीर-रक्षा — Cleanliness, Exercise, Diet and Discipline
topics.description: Daily body-care through शौचम् (cleanliness), स्नानम् (bath), व्यायामः (exercise), हितं मितं भोजनम् (beneficial, moderate food), निद्रा (timely sleep) and संयमः (self-control), and the giving up of आलस्यम् (laziness).

topics.name: शब्दार्थ — Vocabulary of the Lesson
topics.description: Building Sanskrit vocabulary through the शब्दार्थ of key words: शरीरम्, आरोग्यम्, स्वास्थ्यम्, व्यायामः, भोजनम्, नीरोगः, बलवान्, स्वच्छता, आलस्यम्, भेषजम्, वारि and their English meanings.

topics.name: Moral and Ethical Themes — Discipline and Moderation
topics.description: The moral themes of the lesson: caring for the body as the first step of dharma, discipline (संयमः) and moderation (मितता) in food and drink, the harm of over-eating and laziness, and 'a sound mind in a sound body.'

topics.name: व्याकरणम् — Grammar (Sandhi, Vibhakti, Shabdarupa, Dhaturupa)
topics.description: Grammar drawn from the words: दीर्घ and other सन्धि with सन्धि-विच्छेद, the common विभक्ति case-endings, the शब्दरूप of the neuter noun शरीर (शरीरम्/शरीरे/शरीराणि), and the धातुरूप of रक्ष् (रक्षति/रक्षतः/रक्षन्ति).

learning_outcomes.topic_name: शरीरमाद्यं खलु धर्मसाधनम् — The Body as the First Instrument of Dharma

learning_outcomes.topic_name: आरोग्यम् / स्वास्थ्यम् — Health and its Importance

Give the शब्दार्थ (English word meaning) of Sanskrit words drawn from the lesson and use the vocabulary of health and body-care correctly.

Identify and perform simple सन्धि joins and splits (सन्धि-विच्छेद) using examples taken from the lesson, such as शरीरम् + आद्यम् = शरीरमाद्यम्.
Recognise the common विभक्ति case-endings, the शब्दरूप of the neuter noun शरीर and the धातुरूप of रक्ष्, and state the case or form of a word.

learning_outcomes.description: Translate the maxim and the health verses into simple English and answer comprehension questions about their words, grammar and moral.

chapter_summary.title: शरीरमाद्यं खलु धर्मसाधनम् (Shariramadyam Khalu Dharmasadhanam) — Chapter Summary
chapter_summary.intro: This is the NIOS Secondary Sanskrit (209) summary for Chapter 14. It explains Kalidasa's maxim 'शरीरमाद्यं खलु धर्मसाधनम्' — the body is the first instrument of dharma — presents the means of keeping the body healthy (cleanliness, exercise, moderate food, sleep, discipline), reads authentic verses on आरोग्य, and draws simple grammar from the words.

branches.label: आद्यं धर्मसाधनम् — The Maxim
details: Every duty needs a healthy body

branches.label: आरोग्यम् — Health's Value
details: A sound mind in a sound body

sections.heading: The maxim and its meaning
bullets: शरीरमाद्यं खलु धर्मसाधनम् = शरीरम् (body) + आद्यम् (first) + खलु (indeed) + धर्मसाधनम् (instrument of dharma).
The line, from Kalidasa's Kumarasambhava, means 'the body is indeed the foremost instrument of dharma.'
Every duty, study and act of service is done through the body; so guarding health is itself the first duty.

sections.heading: Why health is the highest wealth
bullets: आरोग्यं परमं भाग्यम् — health is the highest fortune; without it no goal can be enjoyed.
The four aims धर्म, अर्थ, काम and मोक्ष all rest on a sound body (स्वास्थ्यं सर्वार्थसाधनम्).
Just as a lamp needs oil, the soul needs a healthy body to act in the world.
Caring for the body is not selfishness but the first step of dharma and of service to others.

sections.heading: How to keep the body healthy
bullets: शौचम्/स्नानम्: rise early, bathe, wear clean clothes and keep surroundings clean (स्वच्छता).
व्यायामः: exercise regularly — 'व्यायामात् लभते स्वास्थ्यं दीर्घायुष्यं बलं सुखम्.'
आहारः: eat beneficial, moderate food (हितं मितं भोजनम्); avoid over-eating (अतिभोजनम्).
निद्रा and संयमः: sleep on time, keep self-control, and give up laziness (आलस्यम्).

sections.heading: Verses on food, water and exercise
bullets: अजीर्णे भेषजं वारि...: water is medicine in indigestion, strength-giving when food is digested, nectar during a meal, poison at its very end — measure and time matter.
The eating-rule हितभुक्-मितभुक्-ऋतभुक्: eat what is wholesome, in moderation, honestly earned.
व्यायामात् लभते स्वास्थ्यम्...: exercise gives health, long life, strength and happiness.
Discipline (संयमः) in eating and drinking is itself a protection of health.

sections.heading: Grammar from the words
bullets: सन्धि: शरीरम् + आद्यम् = शरीरमाद्यम्; दीर्घ + आयुष्यम् = दीर्घायुष्यम्; भोजन + अन्ते = भोजनान्ते (दीर्घ-सन्धि).
विभक्ति: व्यायामात् पञ्चमी 'from', नियमेन तृतीया 'by rule', भोजने/अजीर्णे सप्तमी 'in'.
शब्दरूप of neuter शरीर (प्रथमा): शरीरम् / शरीरे / शरीराणि (subject and object forms alike).
धातुरूप of रक्ष् (लट्): रक्षति / रक्षतः / रक्षन्ति — 'सः शरीरं रक्षति.'

key_takeaways: शरीरमाद्यं खलु धर्मसाधनम् — the body is the first instrument of dharma; every duty depends on it.
Health is the highest fortune (आरोग्यं परमं भाग्यम्); all aims of life rest on a sound body.
A healthy body comes from cleanliness, regular exercise, moderate food, timely sleep and self-control.
Even water helps or harms by measure and time (अजीर्णे भेषजं वारि... भोजनान्ते विषप्रदम्); discipline protects health.
Over-eating and laziness (आलस्यम्) breed disease; moderation (मितता) and effort breed health.
सन्धि joins sounds (शरीरम् + आद्यम् = शरीरमाद्यम्); शब्दरूप of शरीर is शरीरम्/शरीरे/शरीराणि.
The verb रक्ष् in the present tense is रक्षति/रक्षतः/रक्षन्ति — 'he protects the body' = सः शरीरं रक्षति.

glossary.definition: The body; called आद्यं धर्मसाधनम् — the first instrument for performing dharma.
The means or instrument (साधनम्) of dharma; the body through which duty is performed.
First, foremost, primary; in the maxim it describes the body as the first instrument of dharma.
Health, freedom from disease (अ + रोग); praised as परमं भाग्यम्, the highest fortune.
Well-being, sound health; called सर्वार्थसाधनम्, the means to all the aims of life.
Physical exercise; from it one gains health, long life, strength and happiness.
Food, diet; health depends on हितं मितं भोजनम् — beneficial and moderate eating.
Cleanliness, purity of body and surroundings; a chief means of keeping healthy.
Self-control, discipline, especially moderation in food, drink and habits.
Laziness; the enemy of health and duty, to be given up (त्यजामः) for an active life.
Free from disease, healthy (निर् + रोग); the one who cares for the body becomes नीरोग.

worksheet.title: Worksheet — शरीरमाद्यं खलु धर्मसाधनम् (NIOS Sanskrit 209, Chapter 14)
worksheet.instructions: Attempt all questions. Write Sanskrit words in Devanagari and give your explanations in English. Refer to the maxim and verses in the lesson where needed.

questions.question: Split and translate the maxim: 'शरीरमाद्यं खलु धर्मसाधनम्'.
questions.answer: Split: शरीरम् + आद्यम् + खलु + धर्मसाधनम्. Translation: 'The body is indeed the first (foremost) instrument of dharma.' It means every duty is performed through the body, so guarding health is the first duty.
questions.explanation: Word-split plus meaning of Kalidasa's maxim.

questions.question: Give the शब्दार्थ (English word meaning) of each: आरोग्यम्, व्यायामः, भोजनम्, निद्रा, आलस्यम्.
questions.answer: आरोग्यम् = health/freedom from disease; व्यायामः = exercise; भोजनम् = food; निद्रा = sleep; आलस्यम् = laziness.

questions.question: In one or two sentences, explain the moral of the verse 'अजीर्णे भेषजं वारि... भोजनान्ते विषप्रदम्'.
questions.answer: The same water is medicine, strength-giving, nectar or poison depending on the right measure and time of drinking. The moral is that discipline (संयमः) and moderation in eating and drinking protect health.
questions.explanation: Right measure and time make even water helpful or harmful.

questions.question: Do the सन्धि-विच्छेद (split) of: (a) शरीरमाद्यम् (b) दीर्घायुष्यम्.
questions.answer: (a) शरीरमाद्यम् = शरीरम् + आद्यम्. (b) दीर्घायुष्यम् = दीर्घ + आयुष्यम् (अ + आ = आ, दीर्घ-सन्धि).
questions.explanation: Splitting a joined form is सन्धि-विच्छेद.

questions.question: State the विभक्ति (case) and meaning-role for each: व्यायामात्, नियमेन, भोजने.
questions.answer: व्यायामात् = पञ्चमी (ablative) → 'from exercise'. नियमेन = तृतीया (instrumental) → 'by rule / regularly'. भोजने = सप्तमी (locative) → 'during a meal'.
questions.explanation: पञ्चमी shows source, तृतीया means, सप्तमी place/time.

questions.question: Explain the maxim 'शरीरमाद्यं खलु धर्मसाधनम्'. Why is the body called the first instrument of dharma, and how should a student care for it?
questions.answer:
Kalidasa's maxim means 'the body is indeed the foremost instrument of dharma.' Whatever duty (धर्म), study (अध्ययनम्) or service (सेवा) a person wishes to do, it can be done only through a healthy body; a weak or diseased body cannot fulfil even the noblest wish. That is why guarding health is the very first duty.
A student can care for the body by rising early, bathing and keeping clean (शौचम्), exercising regularly (व्यायामः), eating beneficial and moderate food (हितं मितं भोजनम्), sleeping on time (निद्रा), practising self-control (संयमः) and giving up laziness (आलस्यम्). By these simple habits the body stays नीरोग (disease-free) and strong, and can then serve family, society and nation.
questions.explanation: Meaning of the maxim plus practical body-care.

questions.question: Write three simple Sanskrit sentences (in Devanagari) about caring for the body, and give their English meanings.
questions.answer:
1. वयं प्रातः व्यायामं कुर्मः। (We exercise in the morning.)
2. सः हितं मितं च भोजनं खादति। (He eats beneficial and moderate food.)
3. नीरोगः जनः स्वं कर्तव्यं करोति। (A healthy person does his duty.)
Together they say: we should exercise, eat moderate wholesome food, and stay healthy so as to do our duty.
questions.explanation: Simple correct sentences using lesson vocabulary and verbs.

questions.question: Translate: 'व्यायामात् लभते स्वास्थ्यं दीर्घायुष्यं बलं सुखम्' and state its moral.
questions.answer: Translation: 'From (regular) exercise one obtains health (स्वास्थ्यम्), long life (दीर्घायुष्यम्), strength (बलम्) and happiness (सुखम्).' Moral: daily exercise keeps the body active and gives health, long life and strength; the body must not be kept idle.
questions.explanation: व्यायामात् is ablative 'from exercise'; the verse praises exercise.

questions.question: Why is 'आरोग्यं परमं भाग्यम्' said? Explain in one or two sentences.
questions.answer: It means 'health is the highest fortune.' Wealth, learning and honour cannot be enjoyed by one who is always ill, and all the aims of life (धर्म, अर्थ, काम, मोक्ष) rest on a sound body — so health is the greatest of all treasures.
questions.explanation: Health is the base on which every other good rests.

questions.explanation: The chief habits of a healthy person.

What does the maxim 'शरीरमाद्यं खलु धर्मसाधनम्' mean, and who wrote it?
questions.answer: It means 'the body is indeed the first (foremost) instrument of dharma.' It was written by the poet Kalidasa in his epic Kumarasambhava.
questions.explanation: Meaning plus author of the maxim.

questions.question: Why is the body called the 'first instrument of dharma'?
questions.answer: Because every duty, study and act of service is performed through the body. A weak or diseased body cannot fulfil even the noblest wish, so a healthy body is the first requirement for doing one's dharma.
questions.explanation: The body is the tool by which duty is done.

questions.question: Explain the saying 'आरोग्यं परमं भाग्यम्' in one sentence.
questions.answer: It means 'health is the highest fortune' — no wealth, learning or honour can be enjoyed by one who is always ill, so health is the greatest of all blessings.

questions.question: How do the four aims of life depend on the body?
questions.answer: The four aims — धर्म (duty), अर्थ (wealth), काम (desire) and मोक्ष (liberation) — can all be pursued only by a living, healthy body; 'स्वास्थ्यं सर्वार्थसाधनम्' — well-being is the means to all aims.
questions.explanation: All पुरुषार्थ rest on a sound body.

questions.question: List four daily habits of a healthy person from the lesson.
questions.answer: Rising early (प्रातः उत्थानम्), bathing and cleanliness (स्नानम्/शौचम्), regular exercise (व्यायामः), and eating beneficial, moderate food (हितं मितं भोजनम्). (Timely sleep and giving up laziness are also accepted.)
questions.explanation: The daily routine described in the prose.

questions.question: Explain the message of the verse 'व्यायामात् लभते स्वास्थ्यं दीर्घायुष्यं बलं सुखम्'.
questions.answer: The verse says that from regular exercise (व्यायाम) one obtains health (स्वास्थ्यम्), long life (दीर्घायुष्यम्), strength (बलम्) and happiness (सुखम्). Its message is that daily exercise is a simple habit that keeps the body active and gives many benefits, so the body must not be left idle.

questions.question: What does 'हितभुक्-मितभुक्-ऋतभुक्' teach about eating?
questions.answer: It praises the person who is हितभुक् (eats wholesome food), मितभुक् (eats in moderation) and ऋतभुक् (eats pure, honestly-earned food). The teaching is that disciplined, moderate eating keeps one healthy, while over-eating breeds disease.
questions.explanation: The three-fold rule of good eating.

questions.question: Give the शब्दार्थ of: शरीरम्, आरोग्यम्, निद्रा.
questions.answer: शरीरम् = body; आरोग्यम् = health/freedom from disease; निद्रा = sleep.

questions.question: Give the शब्दार्थ of: वारि, भेषजम्, विषम्.
questions.answer: वारि = water; भेषजम् = medicine; विषम् = poison.

questions.question: Give the शब्दार्थ of: हितम्, मितम्, नीरोगः.
questions.answer: हितम् = beneficial; मितम् = measured/moderate; नीरोगः = free from disease, healthy.

questions.question: State and explain the moral of the water verse 'अजीर्णे भेषजं वारि... भोजनान्ते विषप्रदम्'.
questions.answer: The verse shows that the very same water can be medicine (in indigestion), strength-giving (after digestion), like nectar (during a meal) or like poison (right at the end of a meal). The moral is that even a common thing helps or harms according to the right measure and time; therefore discipline (संयमः) and moderation in eating and drinking protect health.
questions.explanation: Measure and timing decide benefit or harm.

questions.question: What lesson does 'स्वस्थे शरीरे स्वस्थं मनः वसति' teach?
questions.answer: It teaches that a healthy mind dwells only in a healthy body — 'a sound mind in a sound body.' Physical health supports mental health, so caring for the body also strengthens the mind.

questions.question: 'A friend says health is only the doctor's job, not his own.' Using the lesson, explain why this is wrong.
questions.answer: The lesson teaches 'शरीरमाद्यं खलु धर्मसाधनम्' — the body is the first instrument of dharma — so guarding one's own health is everyone's first duty, not only the doctor's. By cleanliness, exercise, moderate food, timely sleep and self-control a person can keep himself नीरोग. Health is mostly built by one's own daily habits; the doctor only helps when illness has already come.
questions.explanation: Body-care is one's own first duty.

questions.question: Translate into English: 'नीरोगः जनः स्वं कर्तव्यं करोति'.
questions.answer: 'A healthy (disease-free) person does his own duty.' नीरोगः = healthy, जनः = person, स्वं कर्तव्यम् = his own duty, करोति = does.

questions.question: Translate the verse 'अजीर्णे भेषजं वारि जीर्णे वारि बलप्रदम्, भोजने चामृतं वारि भोजनान्ते विषप्रदम्'.
questions.answer: In indigestion (अजीर्णे) water is medicine (भेषजम्); when food is digested (जीर्णे) water gives strength (बलप्रदम्); during a meal (भोजने) water is like nectar (अमृतम्); at the very end of a meal (भोजनान्ते) it acts like poison (विषप्रदम्).
questions.explanation: Full translation of the water verse.

questions.question: Translate 'शरीरमाद्यं खलु धर्मसाधनम्' and give its moral in one phrase.
questions.answer: 'The body is indeed the first (foremost) instrument of dharma.' Moral in one phrase: guard your health first, for every duty depends on it.

questions.question: Do the सन्धि-विच्छेद of: (a) शरीरमाद्यम् (b) भोजनान्ते.
questions.answer: (a) शरीरमाद्यम् = शरीरम् + आद्यम्. (b) भोजनान्ते = भोजन + अन्ते (अ + अ = आ).

questions.question: Join by sandhi: (a) दीर्घ + आयुष्यम् (b) सर्व + अर्थ.
questions.answer: (a) दीर्घ + आयुष्यम् = दीर्घायुष्यम् (अ + आ = आ). (b) सर्व + अर्थ = सर्वार्थ (अ + अ = आ).

questions.question: What is दीर्घ-सन्धि? Give one example from the lesson.
questions.answer: दीर्घ-सन्धि is the rule by which a short vowel meeting a similar vowel merges into a single long vowel. Example: दीर्घ + आयुष्यम् = दीर्घायुष्यम् (अ + आ = आ).

questions.question: Write the शब्दरूप of the neuter noun शरीर in प्रथमा (all three numbers).
questions.answer: प्रथमा: एकवचन शरीरम्, द्विवचन शरीरे, बहुवचन शरीराणि.

questions.question: Write the धातुरूप of रक्ष् in लट्-लकार (present tense), all three numbers of प्रथम-पुरुष.
questions.answer: प्रथम-पुरुष: एकवचन रक्षति, द्विवचन रक्षतः, बहुवचन रक्षन्ति. ('सः शरीरं रक्षति' = he protects the body.)

questions.question: State the विभक्ति (case) and English sense of: व्यायामात्, भोजने.
questions.answer: व्यायामात् = पञ्चमी (ablative), 'from exercise'. भोजने = सप्तमी (locative), 'during/in a meal'.

questions.question: Explain the maxim 'शरीरमाद्यं खलु धर्मसाधनम्' fully — its word-split, meaning and importance.
questions.answer:
Word-split: शरीरम् (body) + आद्यम् (first/foremost) + खलु (indeed) + धर्मसाधनम् (धर्म = duty + साधनम् = instrument). Meaning: 'the body is indeed the foremost instrument of dharma.' The half-line comes from Kalidasa's Kumarasambhava.
Importance: Whatever a person wishes to do — perform duties, study, earn, help others, or seek liberation — can be done only through the body. If the body is weak or diseased, even the greatest wish stays unfulfilled, like a lamp without oil that cannot give light. Therefore keeping the body clean, strong and healthy is the very first duty of every human being. Caring for the body is not selfishness; it is the first step of dharma, because only a healthy person can serve family, society and nation.

questions.question: Why is health called the highest fortune? Explain using 'आरोग्यं परमं भाग्यम्' and 'स्वास्थ्यं सर्वार्थसाधनम्'.
questions.answer: 'आरोग्यं परमं भाग्यम्' means health is the highest fortune, and 'स्वास्थ्यं सर्वार्थसाधनम्' means sound well-being is the means to all the aims of life. Wealth, learning, friends and honour are valuable, but a person who is constantly ill cannot enjoy any of them. The four aims of life — धर्म (duty), अर्थ (wealth), काम (desire) and मोक्ष (liberation) — all rest on a healthy body. Just as a lamp needs oil to give light, the soul needs a sound body to act in the world. A rich but sick man cannot enjoy his riches, while a poor but healthy man can work, learn and be happy. For all these reasons the wise call health the greatest of all treasures, higher even than wealth.
questions.explanation: Health as the base of all goals.

questions.question: Describe the daily routine and habits that keep the body healthy, as taught in the lesson.
questions.answer: The lesson describes a healthy person's day: he rises in the early morning (प्रातःकाले उत्तिष्ठति), bathes (स्नानं करोति) and wears clean clothes (शुद्धं वस्त्रं धारयति), thus keeping cleanliness (शौचम्/स्वच्छता). He exercises regularly (नियमेन व्यायामं करोति), because 'व्यायामात् लभते स्वास्थ्यम्' — exercise gives health, long life and strength. He eats beneficial and moderate food (हितं मितं भोजनम्) and avoids over-eating (अतिभोजनम्), following the rule हितभुक्-मितभुक्-ऋतभुक्. He sleeps on time (समये निद्रां गच्छति) and practises self-control (संयमः). Above all he gives up laziness (आलस्यं त्यजति). By these habits the body becomes नीरोग (disease-free) and strong, and the person can do his duty well.

questions.question: Discuss the theme of discipline (संयमः) and moderation in this lesson, and how a student can apply it in daily life.
questions.answer:
The whole lesson rests on the idea that the body is the first instrument of dharma, and that it is kept healthy chiefly by discipline (संयमः) and moderation (मितता). The water verse shows that even water becomes medicine or poison according to the right measure and time — so measure matters in everything. The eating-rule हितभुक्-मितभुक्-ऋतभुक् praises moderate, wholesome, honest eating, and the lesson warns that over-eating (अतिभोजनम्) and laziness (आलस्यम्) breed disease.
A student can apply this by fixing a daily routine: waking and sleeping on time, exercising regularly, eating simple food in moderation and not over-eating sweets or junk, keeping the body and surroundings clean, and not wasting time in idleness. Such self-control is not harsh punishment but the loving care of the body, which then serves the student in study and service. Thus discipline in small daily habits becomes the foundation of both health and character.

questions.question: Explain सन्धि and सन्धि-विच्छेद with four examples taken from this lesson.
questions.answer:
सन्धि is the joining/merging of sounds where two words meet; सन्धि-विच्छेद is splitting such a joined form back into its separate words. Examples from the lesson:
1. शरीरम् + आद्यम् = शरीरमाद्यम् (म् joins with आ).
2. दीर्घ + आयुष्यम् = दीर्घायुष्यम् (अ + आ = आ, दीर्घ-सन्धि).
3. भोजन + अन्ते = भोजनान्ते (अ + अ = आ, दीर्घ-सन्धि).
4. सर्व + अर्थ = सर्वार्थ (अ + अ = आ), as in सर्वार्थसाधनम्.
Being able both to join (सन्धि) and to split (सन्धि-विच्छेद) is essential for reading Sanskrit verses correctly.

questions.question: Explain the शब्दरूप of शरीर and the धातुरूप of रक्ष्, with the case-endings seen in the lesson.
questions.answer:
शब्दरूप (declension): शरीर is a neuter noun ending in अ. In प्रथमा (nominative) its three numbers are शरीरम् (one), शरीरे (two), शरीराणि (many). In neuter nouns the प्रथमा and द्वितीया forms are alike, so शरीरम् serves as both subject and object.
धातुरूप (conjugation): the root रक्ष् ('to protect') in लट्-लकार (present tense, प्रथम-पुरुष) is रक्षति (he protects), रक्षतः (the two protect), रक्षन्ति (they protect). Thus 'सः शरीरं रक्षति' = 'he protects the body.'
Case-endings from the lesson: व्यायामात् is पञ्चमी ('from'), नियमेन is तृतीया ('by rule'), भोजने/अजीर्णे are सप्तमी ('in/during'). Recognising these forms helps us read and understand each sentence.

questions.question: Give the शब्दार्थ (English meaning) of eight important words from this lesson and use any two of them in simple Sanskrit sentences.
questions.answer:
शब्दार्थ: शरीरम् = body; आरोग्यम् = health; व्यायामः = exercise; भोजनम् = food; निद्रा = sleep; नीरोगः = free from disease/healthy; भेषजम् = medicine; आलस्यम् = laziness.
Sample sentences: 1. सः प्रातः व्यायामं करोति। (He exercises in the morning.) 2. नीरोगः जनः सुखी भवति। (A healthy person is happy.)
questions.explanation: Vocabulary recall plus use in sentences.

questions.question: Translate the prose passage 'यः जनः प्रातःकाले उत्तिष्ठति... सः नीरोगः बलवान् च भवति' and explain its meaning.
questions.answer:
Translation: 'The person who rises in the early morning, bathes, wears clean clothes, exercises regularly, eats beneficial and moderate food, and sleeps on time, becomes free from disease and strong.'
Explanation: The passage lists the daily habits that make a person healthy — early rising, bathing and cleanliness, regular exercise, moderate wholesome food, and timely sleep. The result of these habits is stated at the end: such a person becomes नीरोग (disease-free) and बलवान् (strong). The passage thus links good daily habits directly to health, supporting the chapter's main idea that a healthy body is the foundation of every duty.
questions.explanation: Translation plus explanation of the prose.

questions.question:
Read and answer:
शरीरमाद्यं खलु धर्मसाधनम्।
(a) Who wrote this line? (b) Do the सन्धि-विच्छेद of 'शरीरमाद्यम्'. (c) Give the शब्दार्थ of 'आद्यम्'. (d) State its meaning/moral.
questions.answer: (a) The poet Kalidasa (in the Kumarasambhava). (b) शरीरमाद्यम् = शरीरम् + आद्यम्. (c) आद्यम् = first/foremost. (d) It means 'the body is the first instrument of dharma' — guard health first, for every duty depends on it.

questions.question:
Read and answer:
आरोग्यं परमं भाग्यं स्वास्थ्यं सर्वार्थसाधनम्।
(a) What is called the highest fortune? (b) Give the शब्दार्थ of 'भाग्यम्'. (c) Split 'सर्वार्थसाधनम्' by सन्धि-विच्छेद. (d) What is the message?
questions.answer: (a) Health (आरोग्यम्) is called the highest fortune. (b) भाग्यम् = fortune/blessing. (c) सर्वार्थसाधनम् = सर्व + अर्थ + साधनम्. (d) Message: health is the greatest treasure and the means to all the aims of life.

questions.question:
Read and answer:
अजीर्णे भेषजं वारि जीर्णे वारि बलप्रदम्।
भोजने चामृतं वारि भोजनान्ते विषप्रदम्॥
(a) When is water like medicine? (b) Give the शब्दार्थ of 'भेषजम्'. (c) When does water act like poison? (d) What is the moral?
questions.answer: (a) Water is like medicine in indigestion (अजीर्णे). (b) भेषजम् = medicine. (c) It acts like poison at the very end of a meal (भोजनान्ते). (d) Moral: measure and right timing matter — discipline and moderation in eating and drinking protect health.

questions.question:
Read and answer:
व्यायामात् लभते स्वास्थ्यं दीर्घायुष्यं बलं सुखम्।
(a) What does one obtain from exercise? (b) Give the शब्दार्थ of 'दीर्घायुष्यम्'. (c) In which विभक्ति is 'व्यायामात्'? (d) State the moral.
questions.answer: (a) From exercise one obtains health, long life, strength and happiness. (b) दीर्घायुष्यम् = long life. (c) व्यायामात् is पञ्चमी (ablative), 'from exercise'. (d) Moral: exercise daily; an active body gives health, long life and strength.

questions.question:
Read and answer:
शरीरम् अस्माकं प्रथमं धनम्। स्वस्थे शरीरे स्वस्थं मनः वसति।
(a) What is called our first wealth? (b) Give the शब्दार्थ of 'मनः'. (c) In which विभक्ति is 'शरीरे'? (d) Translate the second sentence.
questions.answer: (a) The body (शरीरम्) is called our first wealth. (b) मनः = mind. (c) शरीरे is सप्तमी (locative), 'in the body'. (d) 'In a healthy body a healthy mind dwells.'

questions.question:
Read and answer:
यः जनः प्रातः उत्तिष्ठति, व्यायामं करोति, हितं मितं भोजनं खादति, सः नीरोगः भवति।
(a) When does he rise? (b) Give the शब्दार्थ of 'खादति'. (c) What kind of food does he eat? (d) What does he become?
questions.answer: (a) He rises in the morning (प्रातः). (b) खादति = (he) eats. (c) He eats beneficial and moderate (हितं मितं) food. (d) He becomes नीरोग (free from disease/healthy).

questions.question:
Read and answer:
दीर्घ + आयुष्यम् = दीर्घायुष्यम्।
(a) Which सन्धि is this? (b) What vowel-change takes place? (c) Do the सन्धि-विच्छेद of 'भोजनान्ते'. (d) Give one more example of दीर्घ-सन्धि from the lesson.
questions.answer: (a) It is दीर्घ-सन्धि. (b) अ + आ = आ (a short and a similar vowel merge into one long vowel). (c) भोजनान्ते = भोजन + अन्ते. (d) Example: सर्व + अर्थ = सर्वार्थ (or भोजन + अन्ते = भोजनान्ते).

questions.question:
Read and answer:
सः शरीरं रक्षति। ते शरीराणि रक्षन्ति।
(a) Give the धातुरूप form 'रक्षति' means. (b) What is the बहुवचन of शरीर in प्रथमा? (c) In which विभक्ति is 'शरीरम्' in the first sentence? (d) Translate 'ते शरीराणि रक्षन्ति'.
questions.answer: (a) रक्षति = 'he protects' (present, singular). (b) The बहुवचन प्रथमा of शरीर is शरीराणि. (c) शरीरम् is द्वितीया (accusative, the object 'the body'). (d) 'They protect the bodies.'

questions.question:
Read and answer:
अतिभोजनं रोगाय, मितभोजनं च आरोग्याय।
(a) What does over-eating lead to? (b) Give the शब्दार्थ of 'मितभोजनम्'. (c) In which विभक्ति is 'आरोग्याय'? (d) What value does the sentence teach?
questions.answer: (a) Over-eating (अतिभोजनम्) leads to disease (रोगाय, 'to disease'). (b) मितभोजनम् = moderate eating. (c) आरोग्याय is चतुर्थी (dative), 'for health'. (d) Value: moderation (मितता) in food, which brings health while over-eating brings disease.

questions.question:
Read and answer:
रोगी किमपि कर्तुं न शक्नोति, नीरोगः तु सर्वं कर्तुं शक्नोति।
(a) Who can do nothing? (b) Give the शब्दार्थ of 'शक्नोति'. (c) What can a healthy person do? (d) What idea does this support?
questions.answer: (a) A sick person (रोगी) can do nothing. (b) शक्नोति = (he) is able / can. (c) A healthy person (नीरोगः) can do everything. (d) It supports the idea that health is the foundation of all action — 'शरीरमाद्यं खलु धर्मसाधनम्.'
